title: You won't read your notes
hookLine: stop wandering; you won't get to reread your notes, so help yourself now (Meditations 3.14)

cards: A folder of saved articles. Screenshots of good advice. A list titled books to read someday.
Recipes for when life calms down. A little archive of a wiser life, planned for later. Marcus Aurelius had one too: notes, histories, passages copied out of books, all saved for his old age.
In the fourteenth entry of book three he looks at that pile and tells himself the truth about it. Today: you won't read your notes.

teach.b: Marcus opens with a command to himself: no longer drift about. It sounds like someone catching himself planning instead of living.
You won't read your own notes, he says, or the deeds of the old Romans and Greeks, or the passages you copied from books and set aside for your old age.
Some readers hear the Meditations itself in that line, since it's a notebook too: even this, he may never get back to. The reason is the one book three keeps returning to.

teach.h: TIME IS SHORT; THE MIND MAY GO FIRST.
teach.b: Time is short, and the mind may go before the body does. Old age is not a guaranteed reading room.

teach.h: COME TO YOUR OWN AID NOW.
teach.b: So, he says, hurry toward the end, throw away empty hopes, and come to your own aid while you still can, if you care about yourself at all. That's the turn. Notes are only worth something if they become actions.
A recipe saved is not a meal. A line about patience, underlined, is not patience. Marcus isn't telling himself to stop learning.
He's telling himself to stop postponing. And here's the gentle irony. Marcus didn't get his quiet old age; he died on campaign, still emperor.
Yet his notes are still being read.
They could help him only as far as he used them while he lived. The same goes for anyone's notes.

how: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius use Meditations 3.14 against postponing: they pick one saved piece of advice and act on it the same day.

o: a book of prayers Marcus wrote for the Roman people
Marcus's private notebook, which he says he may never reread

games.q: help yourself now — tap the pairs.
p: come to your own aid now

s: Marcus tells himself to stop learning
he tells himself to stop postponing: use what you know while you can.
Marcus died on campaign, still emperor
he never got the quiet old age his saved notes were meant for.
the Meditations itself is a kind of notebook
which makes his line about unread notes all the sharper.

games.q: you've saved ten articles on sleeping better. tonight you could read one more, or go to bed on time. what fits 3.14?
o: go to bed on time tonight.
games.why: Marcus says the notes may never be reread: come to your own aid now, by doing what they say.

practice: Think of your own saved-for-later pile, a note, a book, a piece of advice you keep meaning to use, and pick the most doable one, not the most important.
Picture acting on it: the stretch you bookmarked, the call a friend suggested, the line you meant to live by. Let the rest of the pile wait, without guilt.

wordCard.voice: Meditations, the notebook Marcus kept for his old age, and the very one he says he may never read again. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'reminders, notes': the kind of notebook the Meditations may have been.

carryVoice: Your line: help yourself now. A recipe saved is not a meal. That's day five hundred forty-eight.
